extracted_claims.text: Annex III, point 4 of the EU AI Act classifies AI systems used in employment, recruitment and selection, worker management (promotion, task allocation, monitoring), and real-time monitoring of emotional/behavioural states of workers as high-risk, categorically and without a materiality threshold or small-deployer carve-out.

Under Article 6(3), an Annex III AI system is not considered high-risk if it performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, or otherwise does not pose a significant risk of harm or materially influence decision-making outcomes.

Providers of high-risk AI systems must comply with obligations including risk management systems, data and data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency/instructions for use, human oversight design, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity (Articles 9-15), and must carry out a conformity assessment, draw up an EU declaration of conformity, and affix CE marking before placing the system on the market (Article 16, Article 43, Article 48).
For most Annex III high-risk systems, including recruitment/credit-scoring/education tools, providers may use internal control self-assessment under Annex VI, without involvement of a notified body.

Deployers of high-risk AI hiring tools must ensure human oversight, verify the system has undergone the required conformity assessment, retain and rely on instructions for use, monitor the system, and keep logs; deployers processing special category data (e.g., biometric data) must also conduct a fundamental rights impact assessment.
The AI Act requires registration of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III in an EU database before placing on the market or putting into service.

Under the AI Act, no AI tool may make final hiring decisions without a qualified human in the loop, and using AI to infer emotions, stress or personality traits and assign numerical scores to workers is a prohibited practice.

Starting 2 August 2026, companies using AI tools for hiring, performance evaluation, or other employment decisions must regularly check for safety risks and bias, keep detailed technical records, ensure human oversight and transparency, and continuously monitor their systems.

The European Commission's AI Office, together with national authorities, began enforcing the AI Act from 2 August 2026, when new transparency rules (including Article 50 obligations) also started to apply.

Deployers using AI-driven screening chatbots (e.g., built on generative AI platforms) must comply with both Annex III high-risk obligations and Article 50 transparency rules, including disclosing AI use to candidates before or at the start of interaction.
Following the Digital Omnibus agreement, compliance obligations for standalone high-risk AI systems under Annex III (including recruitment/HR tools) have been formally deferred to 2 December 2027.
Foundational duties such as AI literacy measures under Article 4 remain applicable and are not covered by the Annex III deferral to December 2027.

The consolidated EUR-Lex text of the AI Act as of 27 July 2026 incorporates amendments from the Digital Omnibus on AI, marked as 'NEW' or 'AMENDED' passages, including changes to Chapter XII penalties provisions.

Article 99 of the AI Act sets a tiered penalty structure: up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher) for prohibited practices under Article 5; up to €15 million or 3% for non-compliance with high-risk system obligations or transparency obligations; and up to €7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect or misleading information to authorities, with reduced ceilings for SMEs using the lower of the two figures.

A version of the AI Act text states non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited practices carries administrative fines of up to €1,500,000, and non-compliance with other requirements carries fines of up to €750,000.
Article 100 of the AI Act separately addresses administrative fines applicable to Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies (as distinct from private undertakings under Article 99).

In March 2026, the EU AI Office reportedly issued its first substantive penalties under the AI Act, including a €45 million fine for an opaque AI recruitment system, a €28 million fine for unregistered biometric surveillance, and a €12 million fine for an AI credit-scoring tool that denied explanation rights.
Compliance obligations for recruitment AI become enforceable by 2 August 2026, with potential fines reaching €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover, according to some industry guidance.

For Annex III employment-category AI systems, the applicable penalty tier under the Digital Omnibus framework (in force since 27 July 2026) can reach €15 million or 3% of global turnover for specified breaches, with the relevant high-risk compliance date set at 2 December 2027.

report:
# Compliance Requirements for High-Risk AI Hiring Tools Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act is understood to classify AI hiring and recruitment tools as high-risk under Annex III (low confidence, as this categorical reading has limited independent corroboration), which—if confirmed—would trigger substantial provider and deployer obligations spanning risk management, documentation, human oversight, and conformity assessment (high confidence). Significant uncertainty surrounds the current compliance timeline: while some sources point to obligations taking effect 2 August 2026, others indicate the Digital Omnibus agreement has deferred Annex III high-risk compliance to 2 December 2027, and enforcement evidence remains thin and partly unverified.

## Key Findings

### Classification and Scope
Annex III, point 4 of the AI Act is reported to categorically classify AI systems used in recruitment, selection, worker management, and emotional/behavioural monitoring as high-risk, without a materiality threshold (low confidence) ([Knowlee](https://www.knowlee.ai/blog/ai-act-annex-iii-hr-employment), [Regulation AI](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/sectors/hr-recruitment)). Article 6(3) provides a narrow carve-out where a system performs a purely procedural task or does not materially influence decision-making (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-6)).

### Provider and Deployer Obligations
Providers of high-risk AI systems must implement risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency, human oversight, and robustness measures, and must complete conformity assessment, issue an EU declaration of conformity, and affix CE marking before market placement (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-16), [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For most recruitment tools, this assessment may rely on internal self-assessment under Annex VI rather than a notified body, though this is weakly corroborated (low confidence) ([DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/high-risk-ai-systems)). Deployers must ensure human oversight, confirm conformity assessment has occurred, follow instructions for use, monitor the system, retain logs, and conduct fundamental rights impact assessments where special category data is processed (medium confidence) ([Dialnet](https://dialnet.unirioja.es/descarga/articulo/10126857.pdf), [Questa AI](https://www.questa-ai.com/privacy-cafe/eu-ai-act-countdown-is-your-annex-iii-system-ready-for-august-2)). High-risk systems must also be registered in an EU database before deployment (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-71)). Separately, the Act is said to prohibit AI that infers emotions or personality traits to score workers, and to require a qualified human in the loop for final hiring decisions (medium confidence) ([EURES](https://eures.europa.eu/jobseekers-know-your-rights-age-ai-hiring-2026-08-27_en)).

### Timeline
One set of sources states obligations—including bias checks, documentation, oversight, and monitoring—apply from 2 August 2026, coinciding with the start of AI Office enforcement and Article 50 transparency rules (high/medium confidence) ([EURES](https://eures.europa.eu/jobseekers-know-your-rights-age-ai-hiring-2026-08-27_en), [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/resources)). However, other sources report that the Digital Omnibus agreement has formally deferred Annex III high-risk compliance obligations to 2 December 2027, while foundational duties like AI literacy (Article 4) remain unaffected (high/medium confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass), [GLACIS](https://www.glacis.io/guide-employment-ai-high-risk)).

### Penalties and Enforcement
Article 99 establishes tiered fines: up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices, €15 million or 3% for high-risk/transparency non-compliance, and €7.5 million or 1% for misleading information, with reduced SME ceilings (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-99)). A separately dated EUR-Lex consolidated text cites much lower figures (€1.5M/€750K), which may pertain to Article 100's fines on EU institutions rather than private companies (high confidence, but ambiguous) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727), [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-100)). A news report claims the AI Office issued its first fines in March 2026, including €45 million against a recruitment AI system, but this is low confidence and uncorroborated by official sources ([informedclearly.com](https://informedclearly.com/en/ai/52202/eu-ai-act-first-fines-enforcement-2026)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
- **Compliance deadline conflict**: Sources diverge on whether Annex III HR obligations apply from 2 August 2026 or are deferred to 2 December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus; later-dated sources favor the 2027 deferral ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass) vs. [EURES](https://eures.europa.eu/jobseekers-know-your-rights-age-ai-hiring-2026-08-27_en)).
- **Penalty figure discrepancy**: EUR-Lex's €1.5M/€750K figures conflict with Article 99's €35M/€15M tiers; likely attributable to different addressees (EU bodies vs. private firms), but not explicitly confirmed.
- **Low-confidence claims flagged (below 0.4)**: the categorical Annex III classification without thresholds (0.17), the self-assessment-only claim (0.12), the reported March 2026 fines (0.12), the application of the €35M/7% tier generically to recruiting-AI compliance (0.12), and the claim about generative-AI screening chatbots facing dual Annex III/Article 50 obligations (0.12) all fall below 0.4 confidence and should be treated as unverified.

## Knowledge Gaps
Whether the Digital Omnibus deferral is finally adopted law or a political agreement remains unclear, as does which obligations (beyond Articles 4 and 5) apply before 2027. The legal basis and verification of the reported March 2026 fines is unconfirmed. It is also unresolved whether EU database registration is deferred alongside substantive obligations, which conformity assessment procedure will apply once the extended deadline takes effect, and whether national authorities have taken independent enforcement action concerning hiring AI tools.
